scenarios.scenario: Migrate roughly 500 component files from one styling library to another. Every file gets the same transform, each performed in an isolated copy so edits never collide, and each result is verified before it counts as done.

key.primary: Dynamic workflow: discover the file list, fan out one transform agent per file working in an isolated copy, and run a verify step per result
key.rejected_alternative: An agent team splitting the migration among teammates
key.rejection_reason: Teams scale to a handful of long-running peers coordinated by a lead's turn-by-turn judgment, and teammates are not isolated in worktrees, so avoiding edit collisions means manually partitioning 500 files. A large identical-step migration is the workflow's documented home turf: dozens to hundreds of agents per run, per-item isolated copies, and a scripted verification stage; the docs give this exact 'migrate many files in parallel' prompt.
key.context_boundary: isolated context (per-file agents in isolated copies; results collected in script variables)
key.lifecycle: explicit invocation with the per-run approval prompt; savable as a command for later migration waves
key.failure_mode: Interrupting mid fan-out reruns every agent that started after the first unfinished one, even completed ones; the Large workflow warning (over 25 agents or 1.5M projected tokens) is advisory only and does not pause the run, so cost needs active watching.
key.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later; paid plans; Pro enables via /config

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow: one discovery agent lists the component files, pipeline() runs one transform agent per file with each agent working in its own isolated copy of the repository (worktree isolation), and a verification agent checks each transformed file before the item counts as done.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Subagents with isolation: worktree driven turn by turn by Claude, rejected because roughly 500 items outgrows what one conversation can coordinate and the per-file results would fill the main context long before the migration finished.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness for the structure: the runtime executes the fan-out, the isolation and the ordering of transform then verify. The model owns whether each rewritten component is actually correct and whether a verifier is being honest about it.
sheets.context_boundary: Every file's diff, build output and verification reasoning stays inside that agent's own context and in script variables in the workflow runtime. Only the aggregate result crosses into your conversation; the isolated copies exist on disk and their changes must be brought back explicitly.
sheets.lifecycle: It runs on invocation and in the background until the pipeline drains. It is resumable in the same session, but the replay rule means every agent that started after the first unfinished one re-runs, which is why many small per-file agents preserve more progress than one long agent.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open: verified means an agent asserted the result looked right, not that anything gated it. Scale is the practical trap, since the runtime allows only 16 concurrent agents and 1,000 agents per run, so 500 files times a transform plus a verify plus discovery sits close to the ceiling, and the cost of a full run is large enough that you should trial it on one directory first.
sheets.version_caveat: Workflows require v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan. If you implement the isolation with the subagent isolation: worktree field, note that from v2.1.203 the agent's Bash and PowerShell commands must resolve inside its worktree or they fail, and from v2.1.216 Bash commands that redirect git into the main checkout (git -C, --git-dir, GIT_DIR, or a cd) fail as well; a worktree whose agent made no changes is cleaned up automatically.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow: build the component list outside the script (or from a first enumerating agent), then pipeline() one transform agent per file with isolation set to worktree so each edits its own repository copy, with a verify stage per file before the item counts as done.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An agent team splitting the 500 files among teammates. It loses because teammates are not worktree-isolated, so parallel edits collide, and 500 files is far outside the 3 to 5 teammate range the mechanism is sized for.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The script owns the per-file fan-out and the verify gate, and the runtime owns the worktree isolation and the concurrency cap; the model owns only the transform judgment inside each agent.
sheets.context_boundary: 500 separate agent context windows, each with its own git worktree as the filesystem boundary. Per-file diffs and verify output stay in script variables, and only the aggregate result crosses into your conversation. The script itself has no filesystem access, so the file list must be passed in or produced by an agent.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts on the saved command, runs in the background while your session stays responsive, and ends when every item has passed through both stages. 500 agents is under the 1,000-per-run cap and at most 16 run at once, so wall-clock is bounded by that width.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. A transform agent that dies contributes an empty result that a naive script counts as one fewer file rather than a failure, and a worktree removed while its agent is still running makes that agent's commands error out. The Large workflow warning that fires past 25 agents is purely advisory, so nothing throttles a 500-agent run except the caps and your token budget.
sheets.version_caveat: Workflows require v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan. Worktree isolation carries its own gate: from v2.1.203 a worktree agent's Bash and PowerShell commands run inside the worktree and fail if they resolve to the main checkout, where earlier builds could silently run there, and the worktree branches from your default branch rather than the parent session's HEAD.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow. The script discovers the roughly 500 component files and runs one migration agent per file with isolation set to worktree, so each transform happens in its own git checkout, then a verification agent checks each result before the script counts that file as done.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An agent team. Teammates are not placed in worktrees, so the work would have to be partitioned by hand to avoid overwrites, and a handful of long-running peers cannot cover 500 identical transforms.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The runtime executes the script and enforces the isolation: a worktree-isolated agent's shell commands are confined to its own checkout and error out if they resolve back into the main one, so non-collision is a harness guarantee rather than agent discipline.
sheets.context_boundary: Each file's migration and verification run in their own subagent contexts inside the workflow runtime, against a separate worktree copy of the repo. Intermediate results stay in script variables; only the final summary of what migrated crosses into your session.
sheets.lifecycle: The run starts when you invoke the workflow and ends when the script returns. It is resumable only inside the same Claude Code session, so exiting Claude Code mid-migration means the next session starts the workflow fresh.
sheets.failure_mode: Throughput and restart risk rather than silent breakage: the runtime caps concurrency, so 500 files drain in batches and the run is long, and because replay follows the order agents started, stopping mid fan-out re-runs every agent that started after the first unfinished one. A worktree whose agent made no changes is cleaned up automatically, which can mask a no-op transform.
sheets.version_caveat: Workflows themselves need v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan, and the worktree confinement is version-sensitive: on versions before v2.1.203 a subagent command whose working directory resolved outside its worktree could run in the main checkout instead of failing.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow that enumerates the roughly 500 component files and dispatches one migration subagent per file, each working in its own isolated checkout (a git worktree or equivalent copy) so no two edits touch the same tree, with a verification step (build or targeted test of that component) that must pass before the unit is marked done and merged back.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An agent team, rejected because 500 uniform transforms need no peer discussion at all; a team adds messaging cost and, worse, puts communicating peers into a shared tree, which is the precise collision the isolated copies exist to prevent.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns it: enumeration, per-unit isolation, dispatch and the verify-before-done gate are mechanical steps the runner performs. The model owns only the transform inside each unit.
sheets.context_boundary: One subagent context per file, holding that file and its imports; what crosses back is a pass or fail plus a pointer to the branch or diff, not the file content. The orchestrator holds a ledger of 500 statuses, never 500 file bodies.
sheets.lifecycle: One invocation over a fixed enumerated list; it ends when every unit is done or a failure budget trips, and it leaves behind branches or worktrees that must be reaped, which is state that outlives the run.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on integration. Per-file verification can pass 500 times while the aggregate is broken, because cross-file concerns (shared theme objects, global style resets, a design token file every component imports) are invisible to a single-file unit. Isolated copies also defer every conflict to merge time, and stragglers or silently skipped units are easy to miss in a ledger that large.
sheets.version_caveat: Isolated-copy execution depends on git worktrees being usable in the repo, which is a repository property rather than a Claude Code version gate. The workflow runner that drives the fan-out and the verify gate is the newer piece and I cannot state its exact version, flag or plan requirement; without it the same shape is achievable with batched subagent dispatch driven by a script or the Agent SDK.

scenarios.scenario: Three specialists must run in strict sequence: one finds performance issues, one fixes exactly what was found, one verifies the fixes. Each step consumes the previous step's output, and all three work in the same handful of hot files.

key.primary: Chain subagents in sequence within one session: the main agent runs each specialist and passes the relevant results to the next
key.rejected_alternative: An agent team with three specialist teammates
key.rejection_reason: The three-specialists framing suggests peers, but the steps are strictly dependent and touch the same files. The team docs say exactly that: for sequential tasks, same-file edits, or work with many dependencies, a single session or subagents are more effective, and concurrent teammates editing the same files overwrite each other. The subagent docs document this chaining pattern directly ('use the code-reviewer subagent to find issues, then the optimizer subagent to fix them'), giving each specialist isolation while the caller carries forward only the needed context.
key.context_boundary: isolated context (each subagent starts fresh; the main agent relays results between steps)
key.lifecycle: model-decided delegation, steered by naming the subagents in the prompt
key.failure_mode: Handoff loss: the main agent summarizes between steps, so detail the next specialist needed can be dropped; each returned result also accumulates in the main context across the chain.
key.version_caveat: none for chaining subagents in sequence, the documented pattern carries no version gate; as of v2.1.198 subagents default to background, but Claude runs a subagent in the foreground when it needs the result before continuing, which each sequential handoff does

sheets.primary: Chained subagents in the main conversation: three project subagent definitions in .claude/agents/, a read-only performance analyst (Read, Grep, Glob, Bash), an optimizer that also has Edit, and a verifier, invoked one after another so Claude passes each one's returned findings into the next one's prompt.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An agent team, rejected because the work is strictly sequential, every step depends on the previous one, and all three touch the same handful of files, which is precisely the case where teammates overwrite each other and a single session with subagents is the better fit.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. Claude decides the order, decides what to hand forward, and decides that the verifier runs at all; the harness only enforces each definition's tool allowlist, so the read-only analyst genuinely cannot edit. If the sequence must be guaranteed rather than intended, move it into a workflow script and the harness owns it.
sheets.context_boundary: Each subagent starts with a fresh isolated context containing its own system prompt, the delegation message, CLAUDE.md and a git status snapshot. The handoff between stages goes through the main conversation as a summary, not as a transcript, so what stage two receives is what Claude chose to restate.
sheets.lifecycle: Each subagent runs on delegation within the turn and ends when it returns its result. The definitions persist on disk and are picked up on the next delegation after an edit; an individual instance can be resumed with SendMessage if you need it to continue rather than start over.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. Nothing stops Claude from skipping the verifier, reordering the steps, or letting the optimizer fix things nobody found, and the summarized handoff is lossy enough that the fixer may not receive the exact list of findings. Because all three work the same hot files, they must run strictly one at a time; running any two concurrently risks clobbering edits.
sheets.version_caveat: As of v2.1.198 subagents run in the background by default and their results arrive as a completion notification in a later turn (behavior tightened in v2.1.211), which is awkward for a strict chain; ask for foreground runs or set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1. Background runs also see a reduced built-in tool set, and there is a 200 subagent per session cap from v2.1.212 and a 20 concurrent cap from v2.1.217.

sheets.primary: Chained subagents in one conversation: a finder subagent that reports performance issues, then a fixer subagent invoked with that report, then a verifier subagent invoked with the fixes, each a custom definition Claude calls in sequence.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An agent team. Teams parallelize peers with no worktree isolation, which is the wrong shape for a strict three-stage sequence over the same handful of hot files, where two concurrent teammates would overwrite each other.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. Claude holds the sequence: it decides when each stage is done, extracts the previous stage's output, and writes the next subagent's prompt from it, so ordering and hand-off fidelity are judgment, not runtime-enforced.
sheets.context_boundary: Each stage runs in a fresh isolated subagent context that cannot see the conversation or the previous subagent's transcript. What crosses is each subagent's returned summary, which lands in the main conversation and is re-injected into the next stage's prompt.
sheets.lifecycle: Each stage runs when Claude delegates it and ends when that subagent returns; the chain ends when the verifier reports back. Any stage can be resumed later by sending its instance a message, and the transcripts live under the session directory.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. Because subagents now run in the background by default, a stage's result arrives as a completion notification in a later turn, so Claude can start or report on the fixer before the finder truly finished, and detail is lost each time a summary is squeezed through the main context.
sheets.version_caveat: Sequencing behavior is version-gated: subagents run in the background by default from v2.1.198, and the guarantee that Claude waits for a background subagent's completion notification before reporting its results arrived in v2.1.211.

sheets.primary: A sequenced pipeline of three subagents (profiler, fixer, verifier) driven by one orchestration entry point, a slash command or a workflow, where each stage receives the previous stage's structured output as its input contract: the profiler emits an issue list, the fixer is scoped to that list, the verifier re-measures against it.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An agent team, rejected because peer concurrency is actively harmful here: strict ordering is the requirement, and three communicating peers writing the same handful of hot files would clobber each other's edits with no ordering guarantee.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns ordering if the sequence is expressed as a workflow or a command with fixed steps; the model owns the content of each stage, and critically the model owns whether the fixer actually stays inside the issue list, which nothing enforces.
sheets.context_boundary: Three separate context windows, one per stage. What crosses is the handoff artifact only: the issue list, then the change list with measurements. The orchestrating conversation keeps the handoffs, not the profiles or the file bodies, so the parent stays small even though all three stages read the same hot files.
sheets.lifecycle: One invocation, three phases in order, ending when the verifier reports; each stage's context is discarded at its own boundary, so nothing carries forward except the written handoff and the edits on disk.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on scope and on independence. The fixer can drift beyond exactly what was found, because the issue list is a prompt, not a constraint, and edits to hot files may fix a measured problem while regressing an unmeasured one. The verifier is only meaningful if it re-measures rather than reading the fixer's own claims; if it does the latter, the pipeline self-certifies and the failure is silent.
sheets.version_caveat: This is expressible today with plain sequential subagent invocations, which are stable and ungated, so nothing here strictly requires a new feature. Only the declarative form, where the runner rather than the model guarantees the order, depends on the newer workflow capability whose version, flag and plan requirements I cannot state from memory.

sheets.primary: Chained subagents: three definitions in .claude/agents/ (a performance finder, a fixer, a verifier) that Claude invokes in sequence in the main conversation, each returning its result so Claude can hand the relevant part to the next. No worktree isolation, because all three must act on the same working copy.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An agent team of three specialists. It loses because the work is strictly sequential, dependency-heavy and concentrated in the same few files, which is the case the documentation sends back to a single session or subagents; teammates are not file-isolated and would overwrite each other.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. Claude decides when each link runs and what context to carry forward, so the strict ordering is advice the main agent follows rather than a structure anything enforces.
sheets.context_boundary: Three separate fresh context windows, none of which sees the others' transcript. The only thing crossing between steps is the summary Claude carries in the main conversation, which means the main context does accumulate all three results rather than staying clean.
sheets.lifecycle: Each subagent runs when Claude delegates and ends when it returns; the chain is one stretch of main-conversation orchestration and stops applying the moment the conversation moves on. The definitions stay on disk and are picked up again on the next matching request.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. Claude can skip the verifier, reorder the steps, or hand the fixer a lossy summary of what the finder actually saw, and the result looks complete either way. Because each step returns a detailed report into the main context, a long chain also eats the context it was supposed to protect, and a fixer working from stale findings invalidates the verifier's premise.
sheets.version_caveat: Named subagents need no version gate, but from v2.1.198 they run in the background by default with a reduced built-in tool set, so the fixer's definition must keep Edit and Write; from v2.1.208 a tools list that resolves to nothing refuses to launch rather than spawning toolless.

scenarios.scenario: A support-ops group uses the CLI purely to draft incident communications, never to write code. They want every single response in a calm runbook voice with a fixed structure, and they want the built-in software-engineering behavior gone because it keeps steering answers toward code changes.

key.primary: A custom output style (a Markdown file in ~/.claude/output-styles or .claude/output-styles) with keep-coding-instructions left at its false default, selected via /config
key.rejected_alternative: An 'always respond in this voice and format' block in CLAUDE.md
key.rejection_reason: CLAUDE.md is delivered as a user message after the system prompt and cannot remove Claude Code's built-in software-engineering instructions. Output styles modify the system prompt itself, set role, tone, and default format for every response, and omit the coding instructions unless keep-coding-instructions: true. The docs explicitly route project knowledge to CLAUDE.md and voice/role changes to output styles.
key.enforcement_owner: split: the harness owns the removal, output styles directly modify the system prompt and Claude Code leaves out the built-in software-engineering instructions when keep-coding-instructions is false; the model owns adhering to the runbook voice and structure each response
key.context_boundary: main context (styles do not apply to subagents; only a fork of the conversation inherits the style)
key.lifecycle: Chosen via /config and saved as the outputStyle setting in .claude/settings.local.json; read once at session start, so a change takes effect after /clear or a new session
key.failure_mode: The style silently does not apply inside subagents, and on a style meant for coding work, forgetting keep-coding-instructions: true strips the built-in scoping and verification behavior
key.version_caveat: The standalone /output-style command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91; use /config or edit the outputStyle setting directly

sheets.primary: A custom output style, a markdown file in .claude/output-styles/ (or ~/.claude/output-styles/ for the individual) containing the calm runbook voice and the fixed response structure, with `keep-coding-instructions` left at its default of false so Claude Code's built-in software-engineering instructions are dropped from the system prompt. Select it with `/config`, or set `"outputStyle"` in a settings file for the whole group.
sheets.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md. It appends a user message after the system prompt and can add tone guidance, but it cannot remove the built-in software-engineering instructions, which is exactly the part that keeps pulling answers back toward code changes.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness deterministically assembles the system prompt and omits the coding instructions, but every-turn adherence to voice and structure is the model's.
sheets.context_boundary: Appended to the end of the main conversation's system prompt. It does not apply to subagents, which run their own system prompts; a fork of the conversation is the only exception.
sheets.lifecycle: Read once at session start and in force for every response, with periodic reminders to adhere. A change to the style or the setting takes effect only after `/clear` or a new session, and it stops applying when a different style is selected.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open: the voice can drift over a long conversation, and anything produced by a subagent comes back in the default voice. Dropping the coding instructions is also all-or-nothing, so if this group ever does need code help in the same session they have to switch styles and restart.
sheets.version_caveat: The standalone `/output-style` command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91; use `/config` or the `outputStyle` setting. Shipping the style in a plugin allows `force-for-plugin: true`, which applies it automatically whenever the plugin is enabled and overrides the user's own `outputStyle`; nested project style directories resolve to the one closest to the working directory as of v2.1.178.

sheets.primary: A custom output style: a markdown file in .claude/output-styles/ (or in the managed policy output-styles directory to cover the whole group) that sets the calm runbook voice and the fixed section structure, with keep-coding-instructions left out so the built-in software-engineering instructions are dropped. It is selected through the outputStyle setting.
sheets.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md instructions. They add a user message on top of the default system prompt and can request a voice, but they cannot remove Claude Code's built-in software-engineering instructions, which is the half of the requirement that is currently failing.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, tilting to the model. The harness deterministically composes the system prompt and omits the coding instructions, but adherence to the runbook voice and structure is the model's.
sheets.context_boundary: The system prompt of the main conversation only. Subagents run their own system prompt and are unaffected; a fork is the exception because it inherits the parent's full system prompt.
sheets.lifecycle: Read once at session start and applied to every response until the style is changed; a change takes effect only after /clear or a new session. It stops applying when outputStyle is switched to another style.
sheets.failure_mode: The removal of coding instructions is deterministic, but the voice and structure are advisory: adherence is maintained only by periodic reminders, so long or unusual incident threads drift back toward default phrasing, and any work handed to a subagent silently loses the style.
sheets.version_caveat: No plan restriction or enabling flag. The standalone /output-style command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91, so selection is via /config or the outputStyle setting; nested project style directories resolve closest-to-working-directory only as of v2.1.178.

sheets.primary: A custom output style, a markdown file under .claude/output-styles/ or ~/.claude/output-styles/ selected with /output-style, that replaces Claude Code's default software-engineering system prompt with the calm runbook voice and the fixed incident-communication structure.
sheets.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md instructions, rejected because memory files are additive context layered on top of the built-in engineering system prompt and cannot remove it, and removal is exactly what this team is asking for.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness swaps the system prompt, so the replacement itself is guaranteed. The model owns whether every individual answer actually holds the voice and the structure.
sheets.context_boundary: It replaces the system prompt of the main session rather than crossing into it as a message, so it shapes every turn of that session from the first token.
sheets.lifecycle: Takes effect when the style is selected and persists in the settings scope it was saved to, project or user, until it is switched back; it then applies to every response in every session under that setting.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on tone, and stripping the engineering prompt also strips the tool-use and workflow guidance it carried, so agentic behavior can degrade in ways unrelated to voice. It is also per-configuration, so a teammate who never selects the style silently gets default behavior.
sheets.version_caveat: Output styles arrived in a 2025 Claude Code release and I cannot state the exact version. I also cannot confirm from memory whether they have since been deprecated or folded into another mechanism, so confirm the feature is current before standardizing on it; the append-system-prompt CLI flag is the nearest alternative if it is not.

sheets.primary: A custom output style: a markdown file in ~/.claude/output-styles/ (or the project or managed-policy equivalent) selected under /config, carrying the calm runbook voice and the fixed incident-comms structure. Leave keep-coding-instructions unset so it defaults to false and Claude Code's built-in software-engineering instructions are left out of the system prompt.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A CLAUDE.md instruction describing the voice. It can add guidance but cannot remove anything: it arrives as a user message after the system prompt, so the built-in coding instructions that keep steering answers toward code would still be there, competing with it every turn.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, with the harness owning the decisive half: Claude Code assembles the system prompt, so the built-in coding instructions are genuinely absent rather than argued down. Producing the runbook structure in each individual reply is still the model's job.
sheets.context_boundary: The main conversation's system prompt. The style text is appended to the system prompt at session start and shapes every response in that session; a subagent runs its own system prompt and is unaffected, with a fork the exception since it inherits the parent's.
sheets.lifecycle: Takes effect when the style is selected, but only from the next /clear or new session, because the system prompt is read once at session start. It applies to every turn until the style is switched back, or a plugin style with force-for-plugin overrides the setting.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory drift rather than a hard failure: adherence reminders are injected but the model can still slip toward code-shaped answers on a long thread. The scope surprise is the sharper risk here: any work that gets delegated to a subagent reverts to the default voice.
sheets.version_caveat: No experimental status or plan restriction, but the entry point moved: the standalone /output-style command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91, so use /config or set outputStyle directly. Nearest-directory resolution when nested project directories define the same style name requires v2.1.178.

scenarios.scenario: Policy: no session may ever push to the protected main branch, full stop. A strongly worded instruction file has already failed twice, once right after context compaction. The guarantee must hold regardless of what the model decides.

key.primary: A PreToolUse hook with a Bash matcher that inspects the command and denies it (JSON permissionDecision "deny", or exit code 2 with the reason on stderr)
key.rejected_alternative: An unconditional rules file in .claude/rules/ stating the prohibition
key.rejection_reason: The memory docs state that CLAUDE.md and rules are context, not enforced configuration, and that blocking an action regardless of what Claude decides requires a PreToolUse hook. Hooks run deterministically at the tool-call boundary, outside model discretion, while rules can be ignored, deprioritized, or lost to context pressure.
key.context_boundary: no context window of its own (the hook runs as a shell process at the tool-call boundary, before the push can execute); what crosses back into the main conversation is only the block plus its reason, fed to Claude as an error message so it knows why the call was refused
key.lifecycle: Fires before every matching tool call, evaluated on each Bash invocation for the life of the session
key.failure_mode: A buggy hook fails open: exit code 1 is a non-blocking error, so only exit code 2 or an explicit deny decision blocks; matcher gaps (git invoked through a route the matcher misses) also leak

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook with matcher Bash and an if condition narrowing to git push, whose handler inspects the resolved remote and branch and returns permissionDecision "deny" (or exits 2) for the protected main. Ship it in managed policy settings, and back it with a permissions.deny rule in the same managed file, so no developer can switch it off.
sheets.rejected_alternative: The strongly worded instruction file, CLAUDE.md or a .claude/rules entry. It has already failed twice, and the post-compaction failure is diagnostic rather than bad luck: instruction text is context the model weighs, not a gate the push has to pass.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook runs at a fixed lifecycle point on the tool call itself regardless of what the model concluded, and because it is configuration rather than conversation, compaction cannot weaken it the way it weakened the instruction file.
sheets.context_boundary: Outside any context window. The hook runs as a separate process fed event JSON on stdin; only its decision and the permissionDecisionReason string cross back into the model's context. It fires the same way for tool calls made inside subagents.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires before every matching Bash tool call, in the main session and in subagents, in this and every future session on that machine. It stops applying only if the settings entry is removed, or if disableAllHooks is set at a level that can reach it, which for a managed hook means managed settings only.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed when written correctly, but fails open on every ordinary mistake: only exit code 2 blocks, so a handler that exits 1, crashes, or has a missing interpreter lets the push through with a non-blocking error notice. It also only covers pushes Claude Code makes, not a push the engineer types in their own terminal.
sheets.version_caveat: PreToolUse itself needs no version gate, but two things do. Exit 2 alongside schema-invalid JSON only blocks from v2.1.214; before that the combination was treated as a non-blocking error and the action proceeded. Tamper resistance requires the managed tier, since disableAllHooks from user, project or local settings cannot disable managed hooks, and allowManagedHooksOnly is managed-only.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook matched on Bash, deployed in managed settings, that parses the command and returns permissionDecision "deny" for any push whose target resolves to the protected main branch. The harness runs it before the tool executes, so the guarantee does not depend on what the model concluded or on what survived compaction.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A permissions deny rule such as Bash(git push:*). It is also client-enforced and unbypassable, but it matches command patterns rather than parsing them, so it cannot tell which branch a push targets and would have to block every push to be safe.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. A hook deny blocks the tool even in bypassPermissions mode or under --dangerously-skip-permissions, and it fires before any permission-mode check, so neither a model decision nor a mode change gets past it.
sheets.context_boundary: Outside the model's context entirely: the hook is a separate process that receives the tool call as JSON on stdin and answers with a decision. Only the deny decision and its reason cross back into the conversation, which is why compaction cannot erode it.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires before every matching tool call, for the whole session, in every permission mode, from the moment the settings file declaring it is loaded. It stops applying when the hook entry is removed or that settings file no longer loads.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed on an explicit deny, but fails open on a broken hook: exit code 1 is treated as a non-blocking error and the action proceeds, so a crashed, unexecutable or misconfigured script silently permits the push. Only exit 2 or an explicit deny decision blocks.
sheets.version_caveat: No plan gate. Behaviour changed at v2.1.210: before it, a denied call returned the reason to Claude as a tool error and the turn continued, whereas now the turn ends by default unless continueOnBlock is set. Hooks declared in project settings also require the workspace trust dialog, which is why managed settings, optionally with allowManagedHooksOnly, is the durable placement for a policy that must always hold.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook matching Bash (and PowerShell where relevant) that reads the command plus the resolved target branch from stdin and returns `permissionDecision: "deny"` (or exits 2) for any push that would land on main, registered in managed policy settings so it applies to every session on every machine.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A `permissions.deny` rule such as `Bash(git push *)`. It is also client-enforced, but argument-shaped Bash patterns are fragile and cannot see which branch a bare `git push` will resolve to, so it either over-blocks every push or misses forms like a push with an upstream already configured.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook is a shell command run at a fixed lifecycle event and applies regardless of what the model decides, which is precisely why the instruction file failed and this will not.
sheets.context_boundary: It runs outside the model's context, in its own process, receiving the tool input as JSON on stdin. Only the deny reason crosses back into the conversation, either ending the turn with a warning line or being returned to Claude as a tool error.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires before every matching tool call, in every permission mode including `bypassPermissions` and `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, and is unaffected by compaction because nothing about it lives in the context window. It stops only when the settings entry is removed or `disableAllHooks` is set at the same or a higher scope.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed for the call it blocks, but the hook script itself can fail open: a script that is not executable, throws, or does not decompose compound commands like `cd repo && git push` lets the push through. It also only covers pushes made through Claude Code, so the real guarantee is a server-side protected-branch rule with this hook as the local backstop.
sheets.version_caveat: No feature flag on PreToolUse deny. `continueOnBlock: true` (v2.1.210 or later) decides whether the deny reason ends the turn or is handed back to Claude as a tool error so it can adjust; before v2.1.210 the reason was always returned and the turn continued. In managed settings, managed hooks keep running unless `disableAllHooks` is set there too, and `allowManagedHooksOnly` blocks user and project hooks from interfering.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook matching the Bash tool that inspects the command and returns a deny decision for any push to the protected branch, configured in settings.json, backed by a permissions deny rule for the same command shape.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A strongly worded CLAUDE.md rule, rejected outright: it has already failed twice, and an advisory memory file is structurally incapable of making a guarantee that survives compaction.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook runs before the tool executes and its verdict is not something the model can reason or apologize its way past.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook runs in a separate process outside the model's context window. It receives the tool input as JSON on stdin and only its short block reason crosses back into the transcript as a tool result the model reads.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires on every matching tool call for the whole session, including after compaction, and stops only when the settings entry is removed. Hook configuration is read at session start, so an edit made mid-session may not take effect until restart.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed for what the matcher catches, but coverage is the real exposure: git aliases, a make target or npm script that pushes internally, a force variant, an MCP git server, or unusual quoting can all slip past a naive pattern. Treat the hook as defense in depth and make server-side branch protection on main the actual guarantee.
sheets.version_caveat: PreToolUse hooks are stable, but how a hook signals a block has evolved, from exit code 2 as a blocking error to structured JSON carrying a permission decision. I cannot state the exact field names or the version at which the JSON form landed, so verify against the installed hooks reference.

scenarios.scenario: Our platform team maintains a set of code-review helpers, reusable workflow commands, edit-time automations, and a shared external-tool configuration. Every engineer who clones any of our repositories should be offered the same set automatically and should receive updates whenever we publish changes.

key.primary: Package everything as a plugin, distribute it through a plugin marketplace (marketplace.json in a git repo), and reference it from each repository's .claude/settings.json via extraKnownMarketplaces plus enabledPlugins so teammates are prompted on workspace trust
key.rejected_alternative: Commit the raw .claude/ directories (commands/, agents/, skills/, hooks in settings.json) into every repository
key.rejection_reason: Standalone .claude/ configuration is documented as per-project, unversioned, and manually copied to share. The docs designate plugins plus marketplaces for exactly this need: sharing with teammates, versioned releases, reuse across projects, and automatic update tracking, with extraKnownMarketplaces prompting collaborators to install when they trust the project folder.
key.context_boundary: no context window for the distribution layer (marketplace registration, install, and update tracking are harness operations that never enter a conversation); once a teammate enables the plugin, each bundled component crosses into their sessions under its own rules, for example skills are model-invoked from task context while hooks fire on harness events
key.lifecycle: marketplace registration is offered when a teammate trusts the repo folder; plugins install and enable per enabledPlugins; updates flow via /plugin marketplace update and the plugin's version resolution
key.failure_mode: a version string pinned in plugin.json that nobody bumps means pushed changes never reach installers, and teammates who never accept the workspace trust dialog are never prompted, silently missing the tooling

sheets.primary: One plugin bundling all four component types (agents for the review helpers, skills or commands for the workflow commands, `hooks/hooks.json` for the edit-time automations, `.mcp.json` for the shared external-tool config), published from a team marketplace repository and referenced from each repository's `.claude/settings.json` through `extraKnownMarketplaces` plus `enabledPlugins`.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Committing the loose `.claude/` directory (skills, agents, hooks, `.mcp.json`) into every repository. It ships identical behaviour, but there is no single update channel: each repo holds its own copy that has to be re-synced by hand every time the platform team changes something.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, and ultimately the user. The harness registers the marketplace and raises the prompts, but each engineer must accept the folder trust dialog and the install prompt; the platform team cannot force it without managed settings.
sheets.context_boundary: Mixed. The skills, hooks and MCP tools operate in the main session context, while each review agent runs in its own isolated subagent context and returns only its summary to the lead session.
sheets.lifecycle: Registration is triggered when an engineer trusts the freshly cloned folder, after which the plugin loads at every session start while enabled. Updates arrive in the background after startup only if the marketplace entry opts in, and it stops applying when the plugin is set to false in local settings or uninstalled.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. Listing the plugin in project settings does not install it for anyone else, so an engineer who skips the prompt silently works without the review helpers and edit-time automations, and the platform team gets no signal that this happened.
sheets.version_caveat: Since v2.1.195 every plugin-loading path requires each user to install and trust the plugin, so silent org-wide rollout is not available outside managed settings. `autoUpdate` must be set explicitly because it defaults to false for non-Anthropic marketplaces, and since v2.1.207 `pluginConfigs` from project settings is ignored so plugin option values cannot ride along in the repo.

sheets.primary: A plugin that bundles all four component types (review subagents, slash commands, hooks, and an MCP server config) distributed through a plugin marketplace, with the marketplace and the enabled plugin declared in each repository's checked-in `.claude/settings.json` so a fresh clone offers the same set. One package, one update channel, many repos.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Committing loose `.claude/agents`, `.claude/commands`, `.claude/hooks` and `.mcp.json` files into every repository; it works on first clone but has no update path, so each repo's copy drifts and every change means N pull requests.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns distribution, loading and updating, but the engineer owns acceptance: repository-declared marketplaces and plugins are offered and require a trust or enable decision, they are not silently forced onto the machine.
sheets.context_boundary: Loading happens outside the model. Command, subagent and skill metadata is what enters each session's context window; hooks and the configured MCP server run as separate processes, and subagent invocations get their own isolated context whose result alone returns to the main thread.
sheets.lifecycle: On a fresh clone the repo settings point at the marketplace and Claude Code offers the plugin; once trusted it loads at every session start in that repo, and updates arrive when the marketplace is refreshed or updated. It stops applying when the plugin is disabled, uninstalled, or the settings entry is removed.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open as a standardisation mechanism: any engineer can decline the trust prompt or disable the plugin, so this distributes capability rather than enforcing it. Secondary failures are a stale marketplace cache delaying updates and name collisions when two plugins ship the same command or subagent name.
sheets.version_caveat: Plugins and plugin marketplaces are a relatively recent Claude Code feature and the settings keys for pre-declaring marketplaces and enabled plugins have moved as it matured; I cannot state the exact minimum version or key names from model knowledge, and managed/enterprise policy settings may restrict which marketplaces are allowed.

sheets.primary: One plugin bundling all four component types (skills or commands for the review helpers, workflows/ for the reusable workflow commands, hooks/hooks.json for the edit-time automations, .mcp.json for the shared external-tool configuration), published from a git marketplace repo. Each repository then checks in .claude/settings.json carrying extraKnownMarketplaces pointing at that repo plus enabledPlugins listing the plugins, with autoUpdate true on the marketplace entry so published changes flow.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Copying a .claude/ directory of skills, hooks and .mcp.json into every repository. It distributes the same content but has no single publish point, no version, and no update path, so the copies drift the moment one repo is edited.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, with a per-user consent gate. Claude Code reads the repository settings, prompts each engineer to add the marketplace on folder trust and then to install the plugins, and records skips in that user's own settings. The model is not involved in any of it.
sheets.context_boundary: Nothing crosses at the packaging layer; each component keeps its own boundary. Skill descriptions are always-on listing text in the main window with bodies loaded on invoke, hooks run in their own processes outside any window, workflow-spawned subagents get fresh windows and return summaries, and MCP tool results cross back into the calling window.
sheets.lifecycle: Triggered on the trust dialog after a fresh clone (marketplace prompt, then plugin install prompts), and thereafter at every session start for the enabled plugins. It stops applying when a user sets the plugin to false in .claude/settings.local.json, skips the marketplace, or uninstalls.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open, per user and silently. A repository setting only offers; anyone who declines the prompt runs with none of the review helpers or edit-time hooks and nothing flags the gap, so this cannot be used as a compliance guarantee. If that is required, force-enable through managed settings instead.
sheets.version_caveat: As of v2.1.195 every path that loads plugins requires each user to install and trust them, so a project setting alone never installs anything for anyone else. pluginConfigs values in project or local settings have been ignored since v2.1.207 (user, --settings and managed only), and skipLfs on a marketplace source requires v2.1.153.

sheets.primary: One plugin (or a small set) published through a team plugin marketplace: the review helpers as skills and agents, the reusable workflow commands as skills, the edit-time automations in `hooks/hooks.json`, and the shared external-tool configuration as the plugin's bundled `.mcp.json`. Every repository's checked-in `.claude/settings.json` then declares `extraKnownMarketplaces` pointing at the marketplace repo plus the matching `enabledPlugins` entries, so anyone who clones and trusts the folder is prompted to install the same bundle.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Committing the same loose standalone `.claude/` directory (commands, agents, hooks in settings) into each repository. Rejected because there is no single source of truth and no update path: publishing a change means copy-pasting into every repo and living with the drift.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness loads and updates it, but adoption belongs to each user. Claude Code prompts at workspace trust and records the answer in user settings; short of managed settings `enabledPlugins`, nothing compels installation.
sheets.context_boundary: Mixed, and that is the point of bundling. Skill and agent bodies enter the session context only when invoked or dispatched, hooks execute entirely outside the conversation and cost nothing unless they emit output, and the bundled MCP server's tools stay deferred under tool search until Claude searches for one.
sheets.lifecycle: Triggered the first time an engineer trusts a repository containing the settings, then applies to every session in that repo while enabled. Updates arrive when the marketplace refreshes, automatically if the entry sets `autoUpdate: true`, otherwise on `/plugin update`. It stops applying when the user skips the prompt, sets the plugin false in `.claude/settings.local.json`, or uninstalls it.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. An engineer who declines the prompt gets none of the helpers and nobody is notified; project `enabledPlugins` cannot install a plugin on someone else's machine, and a user-level `false` is overridden by project settings but a local-level `false` wins. Launching from a subdirectory or an untrusted folder silently yields nothing.
sheets.version_caveat: As of v2.1.195 every path that loads plugins asks each user to install and trust the plugin, so a cloned repository can never push executable content unattended. `autoUpdate` defaults to false for every non-Anthropic marketplace and must be set explicitly. Administrators can block the source entirely with `strictKnownMarketplaces` or `blockedMarketplaces` in managed settings, and only managed settings can force-enable.

scenarios.scenario: Our integration suite prints thousands of lines of logs. I want the suite executed and only the failing tests with their error messages to end up in my working conversation; the raw output is useless to me afterward and I will never reference it again.

key.primary: Delegate the run to a subagent (general-purpose or a custom test-runner agent): it does the noisy work in its own context window and returns only the summary to the main conversation.
key.rejected_alternative: Run the suite as a background Bash task and have Claude pull the failures out of the output file afterward
key.rejection_reason: Backgrounding detaches the process, not the output: whatever Claude reads back from the output file to locate the failures still enters the main conversation, so the sifting happens in the very context the scenario wants kept clean. Running tests is the sub-agents doc's named isolation case: the verbose output stays in the subagent's context while only the relevant summary returns.
key.lifecycle: Agent tool delegation: Claude matches the task against subagent descriptions, or you ask for it explicitly or @-mention the agent
key.failure_mode: The returned summary omits a detail you need later, forcing a resume or re-run; and many subagents each returning detailed results can still consume significant main context.
key.version_caveat: none (no version gate on delegating the noisy run to a subagent as of 2.1.220, per sub-agents.md); the background-by-default behavior of the delegated run dates to v2.1.198

sheets.primary: A subagent: define a test-runner agent (an agent definition file under .claude/agents/) that executes the suite in its own context window and is instructed to return only the failing test names, their assertions and error messages. The parent conversation receives just that final report, never the raw log stream.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill (or plain slash command) holding the same run-and-filter procedure, rejected because a skill executes inline in the invoking conversation, so every line of suite output lands in the main transcript before any filtering can happen.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split: the harness owns the boundary (the subagent's transcript is discarded and only its final message is handed back), while the model owns the quality of the filtering, since nothing verifies that every failure made it into the summary.
sheets.context_boundary: The work runs in a fresh subagent context. Crossing in: only the invocation prompt the parent composes. Crossing out: only the subagent's final text message. The thousands of log lines live and die inside the subagent's window.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs when the parent delegates to the agent, either by explicit name or by description match, and stops when the subagent emits its final message. Nothing persists to the next invocation; each run starts empty.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory on content and lossy: the subagent may paraphrase a stack trace, drop a failure, or truncate, and once it returns, the raw output is unrecoverable, so the parent cannot ask a follow-up about a detail that was summarized away. It fails open in that a bad summary still looks like a clean answer.
sheets.version_caveat: Custom agent definitions with name/description/tools frontmatter are a stable Claude Code feature and no paid-plan gate applies, but I cannot state from model knowledge alone which release introduced the model: and tools: frontmatter keys, so the exact minimum version should be checked against the installed build.

sheets.primary: A subagent (Agent-tool delegation) spawned for the single job of running the integration suite and reporting back only the failing tests with their error messages. Either the built-in general-purpose agent invoked ad hoc, or a small custom `test-runner` agent in `.claude/agents/` with Bash plus Read/Grep/Glob, so the thousands of log lines live and die in its own context window.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Running the suite inline in the main session and asking Claude to summarize the output afterwards. It loses because by the time the summary exists the raw log is already resident in the main context window, which is precisely the cost being avoided.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, with the harness owning the part that matters here. The harness owns the context boundary: it gives the subagent a separate window and pipes only the final report back. The model owns what counts as a failing test, so the selection inside the report is a judgment call, not an enforced filter.
sheets.context_boundary: The suite runs in the subagent's own context window. Crossing in: the delegation prompt Claude composes, plus the CLAUDE.md hierarchy and a git-status snapshot. Crossing out: only the subagent's final report. The raw stdout never enters the main conversation and is discarded with the subagent's window.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires when Claude delegates the test run, and stops applying the moment the subagent finishes and its result returns to the main conversation. It is one-shot per invocation: a later run is a brand-new instance with no memory of the earlier one unless Claude explicitly resumes it.
sheets.failure_mode: Hard on isolation, advisory on brevity. Nothing forces the report to be terse, so the subagent can return a long detailed writeup that consumes main context anyway, and once it has returned the raw log is unrecoverable, so an over-aggressive summary means rerunning the suite. It fails open with respect to the terseness you actually asked for.
sheets.version_caveat: As of v2.1.198 subagents run in the background by default, and background subagents are cut down to a narrower built-in tool set. Bash, Read, Grep and Glob survive that filter so a test runner is unaffected, but any tool outside the list is silently removed from the same agent definition when it runs in the background.

sheets.primary: A subagent: delegate the run to a subagent (ad hoc general-purpose, or a custom test-runner agent file with tools: Bash, Read, Grep if you will repeat it) whose task prompt says to run the suite and report only failing tests with their error messages. This is the documented pattern for isolating high-volume operations: the thousands of log lines live in the subagent's own context window and only its final summary returns.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow, rejected because a single test run is one delegated task, not an orchestration of dozens of agents, and a workflow adds a script plus a plan-approval gate for no isolation benefit that the subagent does not already give.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness guarantees only that the subagent gets a separate context window and that its intermediate tool output does not enter yours; what the summary contains, and whether it really trims to failures, is the subagent's judgment.
sheets.context_boundary: The suite executes in the subagent's context window, which starts fresh with its own system prompt, the delegation message, CLAUDE.md and git status. Only the final report crosses back into your conversation; the raw stdout stays in the subagent transcript file and is deleted after cleanupPeriodDays.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs when Claude delegates on your request or the custom agent's description matches; it ends when the subagent returns its summary. Each invocation is a fresh instance, so nothing carries to the next run unless Claude resumes that agent by ID with SendMessage.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and is advisory: a subagent that pastes back hundreds of lines of raw output re-pollutes exactly the context you were protecting, and a chatty summary of a large failure set can be as expensive as the logs. Background subagents also return their result as a later completion notification, so Claude may report the run as still in progress if you ask too early.
sheets.version_caveat: As of v2.1.198 subagents run in the background by default with a narrower built-in tool set that still includes Bash, Read and Grep, so a test runner is unaffected; v2.1.211 makes background results arrive as a completion notification. The 200 subagents per session cap (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENTS_PER_SESSION, v2.1.212 or later) applies to repeated runs.

sheets.primary: A named subagent (.claude/agents/test-runner.md, tools: Bash, Read, Grep) that executes the integration suite in its own context window and returns only the failing tests with their error messages. This is the documented pattern for isolating a high-volume operation: delegate the run, keep the noise in the worker.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Running the suite inline in the main session under a skill that instructs 'report only failures'. The instruction arrives too late: the raw stdout has already entered the main context window before any filtering happens, so the token cost is already paid.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, and the split is where this design is weak. The harness owns the boundary, since the subagent gets its own context window and only its final message crosses back, but the model owns what that message contains, so nothing structurally forces every failing test into the summary.
sheets.context_boundary: The suite runs entirely in the subagent's window. A delegation prompt written by the main agent goes in; a summary comes back. Tool calls, stdout and log lines stay in the subagent transcript, which is stored in a separate file and never enters the invoking conversation.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs when the main agent delegates on a description match or explicit invocation, and stops when the subagent returns its final message. Each invocation is a new instance with fresh context, so nothing carries into the next run and the raw output is unrecoverable afterwards.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. A thin summary silently drops a failing test and the raw output that would have proved it is gone; and if the run is cut off by a rate limit or server error, the Agent tool hands back partial output with a cut-off note, which reads like a short failure list rather than an incomplete run.
sheets.version_caveat: As of v2.1.198 subagents run in the background by default, and a background subagent gets a narrower built-in tool set and returns via a completion notification in a later turn (v2.1.211). Set background: false in the agent frontmatter if the failure list must land in the same turn.

scenarios.scenario: Our project rules file says vendor/ must never be read or searched, and work done directly in the session respects that. But whenever codebase exploration gets delegated out during research, the delegated searches keep touching vendor/ anyway.

key.primary: A `permissions.deny` rule in `.claude/settings.json`, `Read(vendor/**)`, so Claude Code refuses the access itself instead of relying on the model to abstain. As a deny rule the single-segment pattern matches a `vendor` directory at any depth under the current directory, denied paths drop out of file discovery and search results as well as direct reads, and deny is evaluated ahead of ask and allow, so nothing at another scope can re-grant it.
key.rejected_alternative: Restating the prohibition inside every delegation prompt, the fallback the documentation gives for a rule that must reach an agent whose startup context omits the CLAUDE.md hierarchy.
key.rejection_reason: Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model: instructions in a prompt or in CLAUDE.md shape what Claude tries to do, but they do not change what Claude Code allows. Restatement is the documented fallback for getting a rule into an agent that skips the hierarchy, and it is the right move for an ordinary preference, but it holds only while every future handoff remembers to carry it and the tool call itself stays permitted, so it can reduce the violations without making the access impossible, which is what a stated prohibition asks for.
key.enforcement_owner: harness: Claude Code evaluates the deny rule on every matching tool call, ahead of ask and allow, so the outcome never depends on the model reading or recalling the rule; a deny at one settings scope cannot be re-granted by an allow at another, and it governs the delegated searches because built-in agents inherit the parent conversation's permissions.
key.context_boundary: not a context-window fact: the rule lives in the settings files, outside every conversation, and is applied by the harness at the tool call. It still binds inside the delegate's fresh, isolated window, which omits the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, because built-in agents inherit the parent conversation's permissions with additional tool restrictions.
key.lifecycle: Standing and session-wide. Claude Code watches the settings files and applies a `permissions` edit to the running session without a restart, then checks the rule on each matching call from that point on, in the main session and in every delegation alike; nothing has to re-arm it per handoff, and unlike an allow rule it is not held behind the workspace trust step, because deny rules only restrict.
key.failure_mode: Tight but not absolute, at the two edges the docs name themselves: applying `Read` rules to the built-in tools that search files, such as Grep and Glob, is described as a best-effort attempt rather than a guarantee, and the rule reaches Claude's built-in file tools plus the file commands Claude Code recognizes in Bash, such as `cat`, `head`, `tail`, and `sed`, not an arbitrary subprocess like a Python or Node script that opens the path itself. Closing that last gap for every process is the sandbox's job, not the permission layer's.
key.version_caveat: On v2.1.210 and later Claude Code consults path patterns only through `Read(path)` and `Edit(path)` rules, so the search-side prohibition has to be written as `Read(vendor/**)`: a `Glob(vendor/**)` rule placed in settings is accepted but never consulted, and warns at startup. The `Agent(...)` deny form and the deny-then-ask-then-allow ordering carry no minimum version on the permissions page.

sheets.primary: Move the rule from the project rules file into a harness-enforced Read deny rule, permissions.deny with Read(vendor/**) (as a deny rule, that pattern also matches nested copies at any depth). The rules file is not the right owner here because the built-in Explore and Plan subagents are the two agents that skip CLAUDE.md, which is why delegated exploration keeps ignoring it while direct work obeys.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Restating "ignore vendor/" in the delegation prompt each time, which is the documented workaround, rejected because it is advisory and per-call: it depends on Claude remembering to include it on every delegation, and the scenario says vendor must never be touched.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, once the rule lives in permissions rather than CLAUDE.md. Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code and apply inside subagents; instructions in CLAUDE.md only shape what the model tries to do.
sheets.context_boundary: The delegated searches run in the Explore or Plan subagent's own context window, which by design contains only its system prompt and the delegation message, not the CLAUDE.md hierarchy and not the parent conversation. A permission rule is evaluated by the harness at each tool call, so it does not need to cross that boundary to take effect.
sheets.lifecycle: The deny rule applies from session start, to every tool call in the main conversation and in every subagent, for the whole session; it stops applying only if the settings file changes. There is no per-delegation step to remember.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed for the built-in file tools but is best-effort beyond them: Read rules are applied to Grep and Glob on a best-effort basis, and they do not cover an arbitrary subprocess, so a ripgrep or a Python script launched through Bash can still walk vendor/. For OS-level enforcement across all processes you would need the sandbox instead.
sheets.version_caveat: As of v2.1.208 a Read deny rule also blocks the Edit tool on the same path, but not Write or NotebookEdit, so add an Edit deny rule if vendor must also be unwritable. If you would rather stop the delegation itself, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPLORE_PLAN_AGENTS=1 removes the built-in Explore and Plan agents so Claude explores directly under full CLAUDE.md context, and that requires v2.1.198 or later.

sheets.primary: Move the rule from prose into harness-enforced configuration: deny rules in the project settings permissions block covering the file-reading and search tools against vendor/ paths, plus a matching Bash command deny so the directory cannot be reached through a shell grep or cat. The permission engine evaluates every tool call regardless of which agent makes it, so delegated exploration is covered by the same rule.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Strengthening the project rules file, or repeating the prohibition in the exploring subagent's prompt, rejected because that is the mechanism already failing: rules-file text is model-directed guidance, and it is not reliably present in a delegated agent's context window at all.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. A deny rule is evaluated before the tool runs and returns a refusal the model cannot override, whereas the current rules-file approach makes the model the enforcer, which is why compliance evaporated the moment the work moved to a delegate that never saw the text.
sheets.context_boundary: The rule lives in configuration outside any model context and is applied per tool call in whichever context issues it, main session or subagent alike. Only the denial message crosses back into that agent's window. The root cause of the reported symptom is exactly this boundary: the rules file is injected into the main session's context and is not guaranteed to reach a delegated one.
sheets.lifecycle: In force from session start, when settings are read, for every tool call until the session ends. Changing the deny list means editing settings and usually restarting the session, so it is not something a mid-session instruction can loosen.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed for the exact patterns matched and fails open around them: absolute versus relative path spellings, symlinks, case differences, an MCP filesystem tool that bypasses the built-in file tools, or a shell command form the Bash pattern misses can all still reach vendor/. Over-broad patterns fail the other way and block a legitimate read, such as a vendored lockfile needed for dependency analysis.
sheets.version_caveat: The deny-rule grammar and, more importantly, which tools it covers (file reads clearly, search and glob less certainly) have shifted across releases, and I cannot state the current exact syntax or confirm whether this build offers a separate ignore-file mechanism. Verify the rule actually denies a delegated Grep on the installed version by testing it, rather than assuming coverage from the rule's name.

sheets.primary: Move the constraint out of the rules file and into `permissions.deny` in `.claude/settings.json` as `Read(vendor/**)` (plus `Edit(vendor/**)` if nothing may write there either). Permission rules are session-scoped and subagents inherit the main conversation's permission context, so delegated exploration is blocked by the same check that blocks the main session.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Restating the vendor/ exclusion in every delegation prompt, which is the documentation's own suggested workaround. It loses because it is advisory and per-call: it depends on Claude remembering to include the sentence in each spawn prompt and on the delegated agent honouring it, which is the failure already being observed.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Deny rules are evaluated by Claude Code on each tool call rather than by the model, Read rules are applied best-effort to the file-reading tools including Grep and Glob, and subagents inherit the permission context from the main conversation rather than starting with a clean slate.
sheets.context_boundary: The rule itself never enters any context window as text; it is applied by the harness at the tool-call boundary in whichever context the call originates, main session or subagent. What crosses back into the delegated agent's context is only the denial, so it learns vendor/ is off limits by being refused rather than by being told.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies from settings load, for the whole session and every subagent spawned from it, and stops when the rule is removed or the project settings file loses workspace trust. The reason today's CLAUDE.md rule lapses on delegation is that the built-in Explore and Plan agents omit CLAUDE.md entirely, and there is no per-agent setting to change that.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed for built-in file tools and for file commands Claude Code recognizes inside Bash such as cat, head, tail and sed, but fails OPEN for arbitrary subprocesses: a Python or Node script that opens vendor/ files itself is not covered. Genuine OS-level blocking of every process requires enabling the sandbox instead.
sheets.version_caveat: From v2.1.210, file permissions are checked only against `Edit(path)` and `Read(path)` rules. A `Glob(vendor/**)` rule is accepted and warned about at startup but never consulted, so the search-blocking half must be written as `Read(vendor/**)`; and from v2.1.208 a Read deny also blocks the Edit tool on the same path.

sheets.primary: Move the rule off the instruction layer and onto the harness: a PreToolUse hook in settings.json matching Read, Grep, Glob and Bash that denies any path under vendor/. Settings-file hooks also run inside subagents, so the delegated searches hit the same gate the main session does. A permissions deny rule is the equivalent harness-owned surface.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Keeping it in the project rules file or CLAUDE.md. That is the mechanism that is already failing: the built-in Explore and Plan agents skip CLAUDE.md entirely, and even where it loads it is advisory text the delegated agent may deprioritize.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, and that is the point of the change. Hooks from settings files, managed policy settings and plugins run inside subagents, so enforcement no longer depends on the delegated agent having read or honoured a rule.
sheets.context_boundary: The check runs out-of-model, once per tool call, in whichever agent made the call; the hook input carries agent_id and agent_type so you can scope or log per agent. Only the deny reason crosses back into that agent's context.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires on every matching tool call in every context, main conversation and subagent alike, from the moment it is in settings until it is removed or hooks are disabled. It is not tied to a session phase or to whether the delegating prompt mentioned vendor/.
sheets.failure_mode: The documented alternative, restating the rule in the delegation prompt, is advisory and fails open, which is exactly the symptom being reported. The hook fails closed on a match but fails open if the handler errors or times out, and an overbroad path pattern will also block legitimate reads of a vendored file.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate: settings-file hooks running inside subagents is current documented behaviour. The real restriction is tamper scope: disableAllHooks switches every hook off and there is no per-hook disable, and only disableAllHooks set at the managed settings level can disable managed hooks, so a rule that must survive the user belongs in managed policy settings.

scenarios.scenario: The platform team maintains a code-review helper, several lifecycle automations, and a tracker integration that about 40 repos across the org should all receive, with the ability to ship versioned updates that reach every consumer.

key.primary: A plugin (skills, agents, hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json in one directory with a .claude-plugin/plugin.json manifest) distributed through a plugin marketplace, private for internal use
key.rejected_alternative: Committing copies of the .claude/ directory (skills, agents, hooks in settings.json) into each of the 40 repositories
key.rejection_reason: The plugins doc draws this exact line: standalone .claude/ is for single-project and personal customization, plugins are for 'sharing with teammates, distributing to community, versioned releases, reusable across projects.' The manifest's version field plus marketplace installation gives controlled updates; namespacing prevents collisions.
key.context_boundary: no context window for distribution (versioned install and update propagation happen in the harness, outside any conversation); inside each consuming session the bundle crosses into context per component, for example plugin MCP servers start automatically when enabled and surface as standard tools in the main conversation while hooks run as event handlers outside the model
key.lifecycle: Installed once from the marketplace per user or declared at repo level; components load whenever the plugin is enabled; bumping the manifest version propagates updates
key.failure_mode: Fails open at load time: a plugin with an invalid manifest errors (Plugin <name> has an invalid manifest file at .claude-plugin/plugin.json) and invalid component entries are skipped, with the reason visible only via claude plugin validate or claude --debug, so a consuming repo silently runs without the tooling; updates strand the same way: with an explicit version field, pushing new commits without bumping it has no effect and /plugin update reports already at the latest version across all 40 repos.

sheets.primary: A plugin published through a private team marketplace, bundling the review helper as a skill (or agent), the lifecycle automations as hooks/hooks.json, and the tracker integration as .mcp.json at the plugin root, with an explicit version field in .claude-plugin/plugin.json. Consuming repos enable it through extraKnownMarketplaces plus enabledPlugins, or the platform team force-enables it in managed settings so all 40 repos receive it without per-repo opt-in.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Standalone .claude/ configuration copied into each repository. Rejected because it gives no versioning and no update path: shipping a fix would mean 40 pull requests, which is exactly the distribution problem the plugin model solves.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns discovery, loading and version resolution of the plugin's components. Ownership of the behaviour inside splits per component: the bundled hooks are harness-enforced, the skill and MCP tools are model-invoked.
sheets.context_boundary: Per consuming session. Plugin skill descriptions and plugin MCP tool definitions enter each session's context; hooks run out of context as subprocesses. Skills arrive namespaced as /plugin-name:skill-name, which is the deliberate cost of avoiding collisions across 40 repos.
sheets.lifecycle: Loads when the plugin is enabled in a repo and stays active for every session there. Consumers receive an update only when the version field is bumped; /reload-plugins picks changes up without restarting. It stops applying on uninstall, on disable, or if managed settings force-disable it.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open at the distribution layer: a repo that never enables the plugin simply does not get the behaviour, and nothing reports the gap unless managed settings force-enable it. If version is omitted and the plugin is distributed by git, the commit SHA is used and every commit counts as a new version, so consumers churn. Component load errors are quiet too: they land in the /plugin Errors tab rather than failing the session.
