sheets.version_caveat: No plan gate for a self-hosted private marketplace, but submitting to the community marketplace via the claude.ai form requires a Team or Enterprise organization with directory management access (the Console form is the individual path). Passing a .zip to --plugin-dir requires v2.1.128 or later. Managed marketplace restrictions can block registering a marketplace, and --plugin-dir cannot override plugins that managed settings force-enable or force-disable.

sheets.primary: A plugin, published through a marketplace the org controls and installed by each repo or each developer. One plugin bundle carries the code-review helper as a skill or command, the lifecycle automations as hooks, and the tracker integration as an MCP server definition, all under a single version number in the plugin manifest.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Copying a .claude directory into all 40 repos (or vendoring it as a git submodule), rejected because it gives no version identity and no update path: fixing a hook means opening 40 pull requests.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split by component and this is the point to be explicit about. The harness owns the hooks the plugin ships, so those are guaranteed once installed; the model owns whether the skill and the MCP tools get used. The platform team owns the release, but it does not own whether a consumer actually installs or updates.
sheets.context_boundary: Each bundled component keeps its own boundary rather than the plugin having one: hook scripts run outside the conversation, the skill stays out of context until triggered, and the MCP tool schemas sit in the system prompt of every session where the plugin is enabled.
sheets.lifecycle: Installed once per consumer from the marketplace, loaded at session start, and updated when the consumer pulls a new version. It stops applying when uninstalled or disabled, and there is no mechanism to force a consumer onto a new version.
sheets.failure_mode: Version skew is the standard outcome: a long tail of repos stays on an old release, so 'reaches every consumer' is aspirational unless something in CI asserts the installed version. The blast radius also cuts the other way, since one bad hook release breaks 40 repos at once, which argues for a staged rollout and a pinned-version policy rather than floating latest.
sheets.version_caveat: Plugins and plugin marketplaces are among the newer extension mechanisms and shipped in a preview or experimental state at introduction, with the manifest fields and marketplace layout still settling. I cannot give the exact version or confirm whether any enabling flag is still required, so pin the Claude Code version the org supports.

sheets.primary: One plugin bundling all three components (the review skill, the lifecycle hooks, and the tracker MCP server definition without its secrets), published from a private team marketplace with an explicit version field in .claude-plugin/plugin.json. Consuming repos declare extraKnownMarketplaces plus enabledPlugins in .claude/settings.json, or the org force-enables the plugin through managed settings when adoption must not be optional.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Per-repo .claude/ directories copied into all 40 repos. It loses on the distribution and versioning axis: there is no update channel, so a fix means 40 pull requests and permanent drift between repos.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness loads and enables components from settings, so which plugin version is active is a configuration fact rather than a model decision; but ownership of adoption is split, because outside managed settings each consumer still has to install and trust the plugin.
sheets.context_boundary: Per component, not per plugin: the skill body enters the main session context only when invoked, the hooks run in their own processes, and the MCP server runs out of process with only tool results crossing in. The plugin itself is a packaging boundary, not a context boundary.
sheets.lifecycle: Components activate on install and enable (repo members are prompted when they trust the folder) and stay active for every session until the plugin is disabled or uninstalled; updates reach consumers when the version field is bumped and they refresh, or immediately per commit if version is omitted and the source is git.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open per consumer: users can skip the marketplace or the plugin, and enabling it in a project's settings does not install it for anyone else, so the platform team believes 40 repos are covered while some are not. The opposite failure is all-or-nothing: a rejected manifest takes every bundled component down at once.
sheets.version_caveat: As of v2.1.195 every load path requires each user to install and trust the plugin, which blocks silent org-wide rollout unless managed settings force-enable it. Update delivery depends on the optional version field, and pluginConfigs is read only from user, --settings and managed settings since v2.1.207.

sheets.primary: One plugin bundling all three pieces (the code-review skill, the lifecycle hooks, and the tracker MCP server) behind a .claude-plugin/plugin.json manifest with an explicit semver version field, distributed from a private plugin marketplace the platform team owns and enabled per repo via enabledPlugins in project settings.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Standalone .claude/ configuration copied into each of the 40 repositories. It loses because there is no version identity and no update channel: shipping a fix would mean 40 pull requests, and drift between repos is invisible.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness for distribution and update resolution: Claude Code resolves the plugin version, caches it, and connects its components at startup. The model still owns whether it actually uses the review skill on any given turn.
sheets.context_boundary: Plugin skill descriptions and agent definitions cross into each consuming session's context window; hook commands and the MCP server run outside it in their own processes. Skills are namespaced plugin-name:skill-name, so they cannot collide with a repo's own .claude/ skills.
sheets.lifecycle: Components load when a session starts in a repo where the plugin is enabled, and updates arrive on /plugin update or auto-update, which compares the resolved version against the installed one. It stops applying when the plugin is disabled or uninstalled, or when managed settings force-disable it.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails silently open on the update path: with an explicit version set, pushing commits without bumping the field ships nothing and /plugin update reports users are already current, so 40 repos sit on stale code while the platform team believes it shipped. Project-scope components also load only after each user accepts the workspace trust dialog.
sheets.version_caveat: Choose the version strategy deliberately: an explicit version pins updates to manual bumps, while omitting it falls back to the git commit SHA so every commit is an update. For org control, strictKnownMarketplaces is managed-settings-only and is enforced on install, update, refresh and auto-update; pairing it with disableSideloadFlags needs Claude Code v2.1.193 or later.

scenarios.scenario: A production bug has five plausible root causes. We want five investigators working simultaneously, each defending one hypothesis and actively trying to disprove the others' findings through direct back-and-forth, converging on a written consensus.

key.primary: An agent team: enable CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1, then have the lead spawn five teammates who share the task list and message each other directly over the mailbox system
key.rejected_alternative: Spawning five parallel subagents from the main session, one per hypothesis
key.rejection_reason: The agent-teams doc's comparison table is decisive: subagents 'report results back to the main agent only' and 'never talk to each other,' while teammates 'message each other directly' and self-coordinate on a shared task list. The requirement is peer-to-peer challenge, which subagents structurally cannot do; the docs even use competing-hypotheses debugging as the canonical team example.
key.enforcement_owner: split: the harness supplies the machinery subagents structurally lack, direct teammate mailboxes and the shared task list; the model owns actually conducting the adversarial debate and converging on the written consensus
key.lifecycle: Gated behind the CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 env var or settings entry; team forms when the lead spawns the first teammate with user approval; cleanup on session end
key.failure_mode: Fails closed at spawn: without CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 no team is set up, no team directories are written, and Claude does not spawn or propose teammates; a running team fails soft: task status can lag when a teammate fails to mark work complete, blocking dependent tasks, and /resume or /rewind does not restore in-process teammates, so the lead may message teammates that no longer exist; two investigators editing the same findings file overwrite each other.
key.version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default; requires CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1. Behavior described as of v2.1.178 (TeamCreate/TeamDelete removed); known limitations include no /resume of in-process teammates and one team per session

sheets.primary: An agent team: a lead session that spawns five teammates, each assigned one hypothesis, instructed to message each other and try to disprove the others' theories, converging on a findings document. This is the documented use case almost verbatim (debugging with competing hypotheses, teammates talking to each other like a scientific debate), and teammates messaging each other directly is the capability that makes the adversarial structure possible.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Subagents. Rejected because subagents only report results back to the main agent and never talk to each other, so there is no back-and-forth and no cross-examination, only five parallel reports that the lead would have to reconcile alone.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead decides task assignment, when the debate has converged and what the consensus is; the harness only supplies the mailbox, the shared task list with file-locked claiming, and the panel.
sheets.context_boundary: Five independent context windows plus the lead's. Each teammate loads project context (CLAUDE.md, MCP servers, skills) the same way a regular session does but does not inherit the lead's conversation history, so hypothesis details must be written into the spawn prompt. What crosses between them is SendMessage traffic, task-list state, and the shared findings file on disk.
sheets.lifecycle: The team forms when the first teammate is spawned and lives for the lead session. Teammates go idle and notify the lead when done; a shutdown request per teammate ends one gracefully. The team config directory is removed at session exit, while the task list persists locally for resumed sessions.
sheets.failure_mode: Token cost scales linearly with five separate Claude instances, and coordination is where it breaks: task status lags when a teammate forgets to mark completion, blocking dependents; the lead may start investigating itself instead of waiting, or declare consensus early; teammates are not isolated in worktrees, so if the debate turns into edits they overwrite each other. Advisory throughout: nothing forces a teammate to actually attack the others' theories.
sheets.version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default. Requires CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in settings.json or the environment; without it no team is set up and Claude will not spawn teammates. The setup flow described here is v2.1.178 and later (TeamCreate and TeamDelete no longer exist, cleanup is automatic). Split-pane display needs tmux or iTerm2 with it2 and is unavailable in VS Code's integrated terminal, Windows Terminal and Ghostty; in-process teammates are not restored by /resume.

sheets.primary: An agent team: five peer investigator agents launched together, each assigned one hypothesis, running against a shared task with inter-agent messaging so they can challenge each other's findings directly, plus a designated lead or a final consensus step that writes the agreed document.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Five parallel subagents dispatched as Task calls, rejected because subagents are isolated: each returns a report to the orchestrator and none of them can see or rebut another's findings, so the required back-and-forth would collapse into the orchestrator summarising five monologues.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model, at every level. The harness only provides the fan-out and the message plumbing; which hypothesis survives, when the debate ends and what the consensus says are all model judgements with no deterministic check.
sheets.context_boundary: Each investigator holds its own context window and its own exploration of the codebase and logs. What crosses between them is only the messages they choose to send, and what crosses back to the requesting session is the final written consensus, not the five raw investigations.
sheets.lifecycle: Launched explicitly for this one investigation and ends when the consensus document is produced, a turn or budget cap is hit, or the operator stops it. It is not a standing configuration; nothing about it persists to the next bug.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory throughout. Two opposite failure shapes are common: premature convergence, where agents defer to the most confidently written argument, and non-termination, where they argue past the budget without a verdict. Because each agent argues rather than proves, a hypothesis can win on rhetoric with no evidence, so require every claim to cite a log line, stack trace or reproduction. Cost multiplies by roughly the number of agents plus the messaging overhead.
sheets.version_caveat: Peer-to-peer agent teams with direct inter-agent messaging are a much newer capability than plain subagents and I believe they were still gated or evolving at the time of my knowledge cutoff. I cannot name the enabling flag, the config schema or the minimum version, and I cannot confirm whether a specific plan tier is required, so verify before designing around it; a lead-mediated pattern is the fallback if native teams are unavailable.

sheets.primary: An agent team: the main session is the lead and spawns five teammates, one per hypothesis, each a separate Claude Code instance with its own context window, coordinating through the shared task list and messaging each other directly through their mailboxes until the lead synthesizes the written consensus.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Subagents. They parallelize just as well but only report results back to the main agent and never talk to each other, so the adversarial cross-examination this scenario is built around could not happen.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead decides what to assign, when a teammate is done, and what the consensus says; the harness only provides the task list, mailbox files and process management.
sheets.context_boundary: Six context windows: the lead's plus one fully independent window per teammate. What crosses between them is mailbox messages and task-list entries, not raw context, so each investigator's evidence reaches the others only as what it chose to write.
sheets.lifecycle: The team forms when the first teammate is spawned (with your approval) and is scoped to that one session. The team config directory is removed when the session ends; the task list persists locally under the session-derived name.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open, with experimental rough edges: teammates sometimes never mark tasks complete, which blocks dependents and leaves the lead waiting; /resume and /rewind do not restore in-process teammates, so the lead messages agents that no longer exist. Five parallel instances also cost far more tokens than one session, and nothing forces genuine disconfirmation rather than polite agreement.
sheets.version_caveat: Experimental and off by default: nothing happens unless CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 is set in settings.json or the environment. The documented behavior is as of v2.1.178; before that a separate TeamCreate/TeamDelete setup step existed and both tools are now gone.

sheets.primary: An agent team: enable CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1, have the lead spawn five teammates with one root-cause hypothesis assigned to each through the shared task list, let them message each other directly to attack each other's evidence, and have the lead write the consensus document at the end.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Five parallel subagents. Subagents report only to the caller and cannot address each other, so cross-examination would have to be relayed through the main agent turn by turn, which is exactly the direct back-and-forth the scenario asks for.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model, with no enforcement point anywhere: there is no team-layer gate, the lead and the teammates decide what to challenge, what to concede and when a hypothesis is dead. Convergence is a behavior you prompt for, not something the harness guarantees.
sheets.context_boundary: Each teammate is a separate Claude instance with its own full context window; only mailbox messages and shared task-list entries cross between peers, and only what teammates report crosses into the lead's window. Token cost multiplies per teammate for that reason.
sheets.lifecycle: The team is set up automatically at session startup once the env var is set and grows as the lead spawns teammates; it is scoped to that one session (one team, no nesting) and the team config directory is removed when the session ends, though the task list persists locally.
sheets.failure_mode: Stalls rather than errors: teammates sometimes fail to mark tasks complete and block dependents, an idle teammate can sit holding an assigned hypothesis, /resume does not restore in-process teammates, and shutdown waits for in-flight calls. The lead can also declare consensus that is really just the loudest teammate, since nothing verifies the disproof actually happened.
sheets.version_caveat: This is the only mechanism here that is not stable: agent teams are experimental and off unless CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 is set in settings.json or the environment. The implicit no-setup lifecycle described here requires v2.1.178 or later (TeamCreate and TeamDelete no longer exist), and split-pane display needs tmux or iTerm2.

scenarios.scenario: Our path-based blocks stop the agent's own file tools from reading ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh, but a Python script it launches can still open those files directly. We need every process the agent spawns, including children of children, to be physically unable to read those paths.

key.primary: Enable the Bash sandbox (sandbox.enabled) with sandbox.credentials file entries or sandbox.filesystem.denyRead for the credential paths; Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux/WSL2 enforce the boundary on the process tree
key.rejected_alternative: Read deny rules such as Read(~/.aws/credentials) and Read(~/.ssh/**) in permissions settings
key.rejection_reason: The permissions docs warn that Read and Edit deny rules apply to Claude's built-in file tools and to file commands Claude Code recognizes in Bash, like cat, head, tail, and sed, but not to arbitrary subprocesses that open files themselves, and they point to enabling the sandbox for OS-level enforcement that blocks all processes from accessing a path.
key.context_boundary: no context window (the boundary is an OS-level sandbox enforced at command execution time, blocking all processes rather than just Claude's own tools); the protected credential contents never reach any context, and the boundary holds even when a prompt injection has already steered Claude's decisions
key.lifecycle: OS-level boundary applied to every sandboxed Bash command and all child processes at execution time; subagents inherit the parent session's sandbox configuration
key.failure_mode: No native Windows support; the sandbox's default read policy still permits credential files until you explicitly deny them; and unless allowUnsandboxedCommands is set to false, the dangerouslyDisableSandbox escape hatch can rerun a failing command outside the boundary.
key.version_caveat: Sandbox runs on macOS, Linux, and WSL2 only (not native Windows); the sandbox.credentials block requires v2.1.187 or later

sheets.primary: This is not a Claude Code extension problem at all: it needs OS-level isolation. Launch the whole agent inside a sandbox or container whose filesystem view simply does not contain those paths, either the harness's own OS sandbox mechanism (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap/Landlock style confinement on Linux) or a devcontainer with the credential paths not mounted. Kernel-enforced confinement is inherited by every descendant process, which is the property that path-based tool blocks lack.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook or additional permission deny rules covering more tools, rejected because it is the same class of control that has already been shown to stop only the agent's own tool calls and not a child process opening the file directly.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness and ultimately the kernel. Once the process tree is confined, the read fails with a permission error no matter which program in the tree attempts it.
sheets.context_boundary: The confinement wraps the entire agent process and everything it spawns, so it sits underneath the context window entirely. The only thing that reaches the model is an ordinary access-denied error from whatever tool it ran.
sheets.lifecycle: Applied at launch and in force for the life of the process tree, including children of children. It stops applying the instant someone starts the agent outside the wrapper, which is why the launcher, not the settings file, is the thing that must be controlled.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed, which is the point, but it breaks legitimate work: anything that genuinely needs AWS or SSH credentials now fails, and the pressure to punch a hole in the sandbox is the real risk. Coverage gaps remain where a helper daemon, an agent-forwarding socket, or a network service outside the sandbox can be asked to use the credentials on the agent's behalf, and the sandbox story is materially weaker on Windows, where a container is usually the only honest answer.
sheets.version_caveat: Native sandboxing in the CLI is a comparatively recent and platform-limited capability, and I cannot confirm from model knowledge alone the setting name, the supported platforms, or the minimum version in the installed release. If native sandboxing is unavailable or experimental there, a container with an explicit mount list is the version-independent implementation.

sheets.primary: Turn on the OS-level bash sandbox in settings: sandbox.enabled true with sandbox.filesystem.denyRead listing ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh, or the equivalent credentials.files entries, and sandbox.failIfUnavailable true so a sandbox that cannot start halts rather than degrades. Read deny rules merge into the same boundary, so the existing path blocks are kept and reinforced rather than replaced.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook on Bash that greps the command string for those paths: it inspects the command line the model wrote, not the syscalls a spawned interpreter makes, so a script that computes or hard-codes the path inside itself walks straight past it.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, and below it the operating system. The sandbox is an OS-level jail around the Bash tool and everything it spawns, so enforcement no longer depends on Claude Code recognising the file operation at all.
sheets.context_boundary: The boundary is a process jail rather than a context boundary: it wraps each sandboxed Bash command and its entire child process tree, including children of children. Nothing about the policy enters the model's context; the model only sees the resulting permission error.
sheets.lifecycle: It applies to every sandboxed Bash command for the whole session from startup, and stops applying for commands listed in excludedCommands, for calls that use the dangerouslyDisableSandbox escape hatch unless allowUnsandboxedCommands is false, and for in-process tools such as WebFetch that are not Bash.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails OPEN by default, which is the trap: if the sandbox cannot start because of a missing dependency or an unsupported platform, Claude Code prints a warning and runs the commands unsandboxed, so the guarantee silently disappears. Set failIfUnavailable true to convert that into a fail-closed startup error, and set allowUnsandboxedCommands false to close the escape hatch.
sheets.version_caveat: Sandboxing is available on macOS, Linux and WSL2 only and is off by default, so a native Windows fleet gets no OS-level enforcement from this mechanism. The credentials.files form of the same read block requires Claude Code v2.1.187 or later; on older builds use filesystem.denyRead.

sheets.primary: Turn on OS-level sandboxing from managed settings: sandbox.enabled true, with sandbox.filesystem.denyRead (or the equivalent sandbox.credentials.files entries) listing ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh, plus failIfUnavailable true and allowUnsandboxedCommands false so the boundary cannot be skipped.
sheets.rejected_alternative: The Read and Edit deny permission rules already deployed. They lose because they govern Claude's own file tools and the file commands Claude Code recognises inside Bash, not a Python interpreter that opens the file itself, which is exactly the hole described.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness delegating to the OS kernel. Enforcement is a seatbelt or bubblewrap boundary around the Bash process tree, so it holds even if a prompt injection or a rogue script gets past the model's decision-making.
sheets.context_boundary: Enforcement sits at the OS sandbox boundary around the Bash tool and all its descendants, outside every context window. The blocked read fails inside the child process, and only that process's error text can reach the model as ordinary tool output.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies to every sandboxed Bash command and all of its child processes, including children of children, from the moment the sandbox starts until the session ends. It stops applying to commands listed in excludedCommands, to calls that use the dangerouslyDisableSandbox escape hatch, and to everything if the sandbox fails to start.
sheets.failure_mode: It fails OPEN by default, which is the trap here: if the sandbox cannot start because of a missing dependency or an unsupported platform, Claude Code prints a warning and runs the commands unsandboxed. That is why failIfUnavailable must be set to true for this requirement. The other holes are configured ones, excludedCommands entries and dangerouslyDisableSandbox unless allowUnsandboxedCommands is false.
sheets.version_caveat: The gate is platform rather than plan: bash sandboxing covers macOS, Linux and WSL2 only and defaults to false, so a Windows-native laptop gets no OS-level enforcement from it and needs a different control. The sandbox.credentials.files form of the same block requires Claude Code v2.1.187 or later.

sheets.primary: Enable OS-level sandboxing: sandbox.enabled true with sandbox.filesystem.denyRead listing ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh, or the equivalent sandbox.credentials.files entries with mode "deny", set in managed (or user) settings. Sandboxing is the only layer that constrains the Bash tool's child processes, and the restriction applies to all subprocesses including children of children.
sheets.rejected_alternative: More Read(...) deny rules, which is what is already in place. Those cover Claude's built-in file tools and the file commands Claude Code recognizes in Bash, but the documentation is explicit that they do not apply to arbitrary subprocesses like a Python or Node script that opens the file itself.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness sets the boundary and the OS enforces it (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap plus a seccomp filter on Linux and WSL2), so the block holds even against a process the model never reasoned about.
sheets.context_boundary: Enforcement lives in the kernel around the spawned process tree, entirely outside the model's context window; the model sees only a permission-denied error from whatever it ran. Read and Edit deny rules are merged into the same sandbox boundary, so the tool-level and OS-level layers compose rather than compete.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies to every sandboxed Bash command and its descendants from session start for as long as the setting is present. It stops applying for anything matched by sandbox.excludedCommands and for calls that use the dangerouslyDisableSandbox escape hatch.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open in two default configurations worth closing: if the sandbox cannot start, commands run unsandboxed with only a warning unless failIfUnavailable is true, and the dangerouslyDisableSandbox parameter stays available unless allowUnsandboxedCommands is false. Blocking those paths also breaks legitimate work, so expect git over SSH and any aws CLI call to start failing and plan the allowRead exceptions accordingly.
sheets.version_caveat: Sandboxing is macOS, Linux and WSL2 only, defaults to disabled, and has no native Windows equivalent, so a Windows fleet needs a different control. sandbox.credentials.files requires Claude Code v2.1.187 or later, and filesystem.allowManagedReadPathsOnly (managed settings only) is what stops a developer re-opening the path in their own settings, since denyRead merges from all scopes but allowRead would otherwise merge too.
